title: More Applications of Magnetism
lead: The chapter closes on the instruments its results have made possible. A mass spectrometer is the radius of a charged particle's circle read backwards: fix the speed, the charge and the field, and the width of the arc an ion turns is a reading of its mass. The stage that fixes the speed is a pair of crossed fields whose forces balance on one speed only, and that balance is the one new result the section proves. The same steering that bends an ion round a chamber points the beam of a cathode ray tube at the screen, and a field made to vary slightly across a patient lets a radio frequency report where in the body it was absorbed, which is what magnetic resonance imaging is. The section ends with the faintest fields anyone measures, those of a beating heart and a working brain.
summary_html: • Crossed (perpendicular) electric and magnetic fields act as a velocity filter, giving equal and opposite forces on any charge with velocity perpendicular to the fields and of magnitude$$\kv = \frac{\kEf}{\kBmag}.$$
notes: Seventeen of the section’s thirty-five problems are left out because the book gives them no answer, among them its two Construct Your Own Problem items. The link to the PhET simulation Magnet and Compass is left out with the other three of the chapter. The answer to the Critical Thinking problem is kept exactly as the book prints it, although the working there divides by $9.11 \times 10^{-11}$ where it means the electron’s mass of $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, which is why the time it reports is so large.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key. The forty-one exercises the book prints here are the chapter’s review set rather than this section’s own, so each is tagged with the concepts it tests across Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field, The Hall Effect, Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor, Torque on a Current Loop, Magnetic Fields Produced by Currents and Magnetic Force between Two Parallel Conductors, and none is moved to another section. The six conceptual questions carry no answer in the book, so each is kept as an open item with an AI-written suggested approach. Seventeen problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the directions of the fields in a loop and two coils, the field at the center of a motor’s loop, the field inside a solenoid of 10,000 turns per meter, the distance from a car’s starter cable, the wire touching a loop, the second of the two vector-addition problems, the field under a power line, the voltage that accelerates an electron to a given speed, the nonmechanical water meter, the torque on a galvanometer’s coil, the period of a circular orbit, the curving baseball, the wire held up by repulsion, the helium ion of unreasonable charge, the Hall voltage in a blood vessel, and the two Construct Your Own Problem items. Three kept problems lean on an item that is left out or sits in another section, so each quotes inside its own prompt, in the book’s words, the solenoid, the period or the MHD drive it is told to use.

figures.original_caption: This mass spectrometer uses a velocity selector to fix $v$ so that the radius of the path is proportional to mass.

The cathode ray tube (CRT) is so named because rays of electrons originate at the cathode in the electron gun. Magnetic coils are used to steer the beam in many CRTs. In this case, the beam is moved down. Another pair of horizontal coils would steer the beam horizontally.

exercises.prompt: Measurements of the weak and fluctuating magnetic fields associated with brain activity are called magnetoencephalograms (MEGs). Do the brain’s magnetic fields imply coordinated or uncoordinated nerve impulses? Explain.

answer.solution: They imply coordinated impulses. Each nerve impulse is a current, and a current makes a magnetic field; but the impulses run in every direction through the brain, and the field of one impulse points the opposite way to the field of an impulse running the other way. If the impulses were uncoordinated, the fields of the individual currents would very largely cancel one another and nothing would be left to measure outside the head. A field that can be picked up at all, even one this weak, means that many nerve cells are carrying their currents in step and in the same direction, so that their fields add rather than cancel. This is also why the MEG reports activity rather than structure: what it sees is cells firing together.

exercises.prompt: Discuss the possibility that a Hall voltage would be generated on the moving heart of a patient during MRI imaging. Also discuss the same effect on the wires of a pacemaker. (The fact that patients with pacemakers are not given MRIs is significant.)

answer.solution: Blood is a conductor, and the heart moves it across the field of the magnet, so the conditions for a Hall voltage are met: the field pushes the positive and negative carriers in the blood to opposite walls of a vessel until the electric field between them balances the magnetic force, leaving an emf of about $\kBmag\kv\ell$ across the vessel. With a field of 1 to 2 T, a vessel a centimeter or two across and blood moving at a few tenths of a meter per second, this comes to a few tens of millivolts, which is the same size as the voltages the heart works with. The wires of a pacemaker are a much better conductor and they move with the heart, so the same effect appears along them, and a voltage of that size arriving at the pacemaker is a signal it was never meant to receive. That is on top of the force the strong field exerts on any magnetic material in the device. The two together are why a patient with a pacemaker is not put in an MRI unit.

exercises.prompt: A patient in an MRI unit turns his head quickly to one side and experiences momentary dizziness and a strange taste in his mouth. Discuss the possible causes.

answer.solution: Turning the head quickly moves the conducting fluids of the head across a field of 1 to 2 T, and a conductor moving across a field develops a voltage across it, the same Hall emf $\kBmag\kv\ell$ that a Hall probe reads. The fluid of the semicircular canals of the inner ear is what the body uses to sense rotation, and a voltage appearing across it, or a force on the ions in it, is read by the brain as motion that is not happening, which is dizziness. The tongue is wet, salty and well supplied with nerves, and a small voltage across it stimulates the taste receptors directly, which is felt as a metallic taste. Both effects last only while the head is moving, because it is the motion across the field, and not the field itself, that produces the voltage.

exercises.prompt: You are told that in a certain region there is either a uniform electric or magnetic field. What measurement or observation could you make to determine the type? (Ignore the Earth’s magnetic field.)

answer.solution: Put a charge in the region and leave it at rest. An electric field exerts the force $\kq\kEf$ on a charge whether it is moving or not, so the charge is set moving in a straight line along the field. A magnetic field exerts $\kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta$, which is zero when the speed is zero, so a charge at rest stays at rest. If a charge at rest will not move, send one through instead: an electric field can act along the direction of motion and change the speed, while a magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, does no work, and bends the path into a circle at unchanged speed. There is one further test that separates them: a charge sent along the direction of a magnetic field feels no force at all, and there is no direction in which a charge is free of an electric field.

exercises.prompt: An example of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) comes from the flow of a river (salty water). This fluid interacts with the Earth’s magnetic field to produce a potential difference between the two river banks. How would you go about calculating the potential difference?

answer.solution: Treat the river as the moving conductor of a Hall probe. The ions dissolved in the water are carried along by the flow at speed $\kv$, and the component of the Earth’s field perpendicular to both the flow and the line across the river pushes the positive ions toward one bank and the negative ions toward the other. They collect there until the electric field they set up balances the magnetic force, and at that point the potential difference between the banks is $\kemfhall = \kBmag\ell\kv$, with $\ell$ the width of the river. So three numbers are needed: the width of the river, the average speed of the flow, and the component of the Earth’s field at right angles to the plane the other two lie in, which for a river running east to west is the vertical component. A river 100 m wide flowing at 1 m/s through a vertical field component of $5 \times 10^{-5}$ T gives about 5 mV between the banks.

exercises.prompt: Draw gravitational field lines between 2 masses, electric field lines between a positive and a negative charge, electric field lines between 2 positive charges and magnetic field lines around a magnet. Qualitatively describe the differences between the fields and the entities responsible for the field lines.

answer.solution: The gravitational lines between two masses run from each mass toward the other and end on them, because gravity only ever attracts and mass comes in one sign; the picture looks like the electric one for two opposite charges, and there is no arrangement of masses that gives the second picture. The electric lines between a positive and a negative charge leave the positive charge, curve across the gap and end on the negative charge, since electric field lines begin on positive charge and end on negative charge. Between two positive charges the lines leave both and bend away from one another, leaving an empty point midway between them where the two contributions cancel, and no line crosses from one charge to the other. The magnetic lines around a bar magnet neither begin nor end: outside the magnet they leave the north pole and curve round to the south pole, and inside the magnet they continue from south to north, so that every line is a closed loop. That last difference is the important one. A charge can be had on its own, so electric field lines have ends; a magnetic pole cannot, since cutting a magnet in half gives two magnets rather than a north and a south, so magnetic field lines have none.

exercises.prompt: To see why an MRI utilizes iron to increase the magnetic field created by a coil, calculate the current needed in a 400-loop-per-meter circular coil 0.660 m in radius to create a 1.20-T field (typical of an MRI instrument) at its center with no iron present. The magnetic field of a proton is approximately like that of a circular current loop $0.650 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ in radius carrying $1.05 \times 10^{4}\ \text{A}$. What is the field at the center of such a loop?

answer.part: the field at the center of the proton’s loop
answer.hint: The field at the center of a single loop is $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\kR$. For the coil, which is many loops to the meter, use $\kBmag = \mu_0 n\kIcur$ instead and solve it for the current.

exercises.prompt: Nonnuclear submarines use batteries for power when submerged. (a) Find the magnetic field 50.0 cm from a straight wire carrying 1200 A from the batteries to the drive mechanism of a submarine. (b) What is the field if the wires to and from the drive mechanism are side by side? (c) Discuss the effects this could have for a compass on the submarine that is not shielded.

parts.hint: The field of a long straight wire is $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\pi\kr$, with $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$.
The two wires carry the same current in opposite directions. Work out which way each one sends its field at a point beside the pair and add the two contributions.

answer.solution: (a) $4.80 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$ (b) Zero (c) If the wires are not paired, the field is about 10 times stronger than Earth’s magnetic field and so could severely disrupt the use of a compass.

exercises.prompt: What current is needed in the solenoid described in the preceding problem — “How strong is the magnetic field inside a solenoid with 10,000 turns per meter that carries 20.0 A?” — to produce a magnetic field $10^{4}$ times the Earth’s magnetic field of $5.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$?

answer.hint: The field inside a solenoid is $\kBmag = \mu_0 n\kIcur$, with $n$ the number of turns per meter. Work out the field that is wanted first, then solve for the current.

exercises.prompt: Measurements affect the system being measured, such as the current loop in Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor. (a) Estimate the field the loop creates by calculating the field at the center of a circular loop 20.0 cm in diameter carrying 5.00 A. (b) What is the smallest field strength this loop can be used to measure, if its field must alter the measured field by less than 0.0100%?

parts.hint: At the center of a single loop the field is $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\kR$, and $\kR$ is half the diameter.
The loop’s own field must be less than 0.0100% of the field being measured, so divide the answer to (a) by that fraction written as a decimal.

exercises.prompt: Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at the point equidistant from the wires in the figure below (a), using the rules of vector addition to sum the contributions from each wire.

answer.hint: The point equidistant from the three wires is the center of the triangle, a distance $\kr = a/\sqrt{3}$ from each of them with $a$ the side. Work out $\mu_0\kIcur/2\pi\kr$ for each wire, point each contribution at right angles to the line from its wire using right hand rule 2, and add the three as vectors.

exercises.prompt: What current is needed in the top wire in the figure above (a) to produce a field of zero at the point equidistant from the wires, if the currents in the bottom two wires are both 10.0 A into the page?

answer.hint: All three wires are the same distance from the point, so each contributes a field proportional to its own current. Add the two equal contributions from the bottom wires as vectors first, and ask what the third wire must supply to cancel the result.

exercises.prompt: (a) A pendulum is set up so that its bob (a thin copper disk) swings between the poles of a permanent magnet as shown in the figure below. What is the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force on the bob at the lowest point in its path, if it has a positive $0.250\ \mu\text{C}$ charge and is released from a height of 30.0 cm above its lowest point? The magnetic field strength is 1.50 T. (b) What is the acceleration of the bob at the bottom of its swing if its mass is 30.0 grams and it is hung from a flexible string? Be certain to include a free-body diagram as part of your analysis.

parts.hint: Conservation of energy gives the speed at the bottom, $\kv = \sqrt{2\kg\kh}$, and the force is then $\kF = \kq\kv\kBmag$, since the velocity at the lowest point is perpendicular to the field.
The string is flexible, so it can supply no force along the direction of the magnetic force. Newton’s second law along that direction gives the acceleration as the magnetic force divided by the mass.

exercises.prompt: Find the radius of curvature of the path of a 25.0-MeV proton moving perpendicularly to the 1.20-T field of a cyclotron.

answer.hint: Turn the energy into a speed first: 1 MeV is $1.60 \times 10^{-13}$ J, and $\kKE = \tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ for a proton of mass $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg. Then $\kr = m\kv/\kq\kBmag$.

exercises.prompt: (a) Using the values given for an MHD drive in Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor — “What force is exerted on the water in an MHD drive utilizing a 25.0-cm-diameter tube, if 100-A current is passed across the tube that is perpendicular to a 2.00-T magnetic field?” — and assuming the force is uniformly applied to the fluid, calculate the pressure created in $\text{N/m}^{2}$. (b) Is this a significant fraction of an atmosphere?

parts.hint: The force on the fluid is $\kF = \kIcur\ell\kBmag$ with $\ell$ the diameter of the tube, and a pressure is a force divided by the area it acts over, here the cross section of the tube.

answer.solution: (a) $1.02 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N/m}^2$ (b) Not a significant fraction of an atmosphere

exercises.prompt: A current balance used to define the ampere is designed so that the current through it is constant, as is the distance between wires. Even so, if the wires change length with temperature, the force between them will change. What percent change in force per degree will occur if the wires are copper?

answer.hint: With the currents and the separation held fixed, the force is proportional to the length of wire in the field, so the fractional change in the force is the fractional change in the length, $\Delta L/L = \alpha\Delta T$ with copper’s coefficient of linear expansion.

figure.caption: Cyclotrons accelerate charged particles orbiting in a magnetic field by placing an AC voltage on the metal Dees, between which the particles move, so that energy is added twice each orbit. The frequency is constant, since it is independent of the particle energy—the radius of the orbit simply increases with energy until the particles approach the edge and are extracted for various experiments and applications.

exercises.prompt: A cyclotron accelerates charged particles as shown in the figure below. Using the results of the previous problem — the period of the circular orbit of a charged particle moving perpendicularly to a uniform magnetic field is $T = 2\pi m/(qB)$ — calculate the frequency of the accelerating voltage needed for a proton in a 1.20-T field.

answer.hint: The frequency is one over the period, so $f = \kq\kBmag/2\pi m$. A proton has a mass of $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg and a charge of $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C, and neither the speed nor the radius of the orbit enters.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the direction of the force on a wire carrying a current due east in a location where the Earth’s field is due north? Both are parallel to the ground. (b) Calculate the force per meter if the wire carries 20.0 A and the field strength is $3.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. (c) What diameter copper wire would have its weight supported by this force? (d) Calculate the resistance per meter and the voltage per meter needed.

parts.hint: The current and the field are at right angles, so the force per unit length is $\kF/\ell = \kIcur\kBmag$.
Set the weight of a meter of wire, its density times its cross-sectional area times $\kg$, equal to the force per meter from (b), and solve for the diameter.
Use $\kRes = \rho L/A$ with copper’s resistivity and the cross section that belongs to the diameter found in (c).
Ohm’s law on one meter of the wire: the voltage per meter is the current times the resistance per meter.

exercises.prompt: (a) Find the charge on a baseball, thrown at 35.0 m/s perpendicular to the Earth’s $5.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ field, that experiences a 1.00-N magnetic force. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumption or premise is responsible?

parts.hint: Solve $\kF = \kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta$ for the charge, with the angle a right angle so that the sine is one.

answer.solution: (a) 571 C (b) Impossible to have such a large separated charge on such a small object. (c) The 1.00-N force is much too great to be realistic in the Earth’s field.

exercises.prompt: An inventor wants to generate 120-V power by moving a 1.00-m-long wire perpendicular to the Earth’s $5.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ field. (a) Find the speed with which the wire must move. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumption is responsible?

parts.hint: A conductor of length $\ell$ moving at speed $\kv$ across a field $\kBmag$ develops $\kemfhall = \kBmag\ell\kv$ across it. Solve that for the speed.

answer.solution: (a) $2.40 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$ (b) The speed is too high to be practical, since it is more than 1% of the speed of light. (c) The assumption that you could reasonably generate such a voltage with a single wire in the Earth’s field is unreasonable.

exercises.prompt: A surveyor 100 m from a long straight 200-kV DC power line suspects that its magnetic field may equal that of the Earth and affect compass readings. (a) Calculate the current in the wire needed to create a $5.00 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ field at this distance. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumption or premise is responsible?

parts.hint: Solve the field of a long straight wire, $\kBmag = \mu_0\kIcur/2\pi\kr$, for the current.

answer.solution: (a) 25.0 kA (b) This current is unreasonably high. It implies a total power delivery in the line of $50.0 \times 10^{9}$ W, which is much too high for standard transmission lines. (c) 100 meters is a long distance to obtain the required field strength. Also coaxial cables are used for transmission lines so that there is virtually no field for DC power lines, because of cancellation from opposing currents. The surveyor’s concerns are not a problem for his magnetic field measurements.

exercises.prompt: A magnetic field of $2.00 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}$ in the positive x-direction exists. Three electrons pass through the origin, one at a time, each with a velocity of $5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s}$. The first electron passes the origin along the x-axis, the second electron along the y-axis, and the third at an angle of $45^\circ$ with respect to both the y- and z-axes in the yz-plane. (a) What is the force acting on each electron? (b) What is the shape of the path of each electron? (c) When, if ever, will each electron return to the origin?

answer.solution: (a) $F = qvB\sin\theta$. Since $\sin\theta = 0$, $F = 0$ for the first electron. For the second and third electrons, $\sin\theta = 1$. So $F = (1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C})(5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m/s})(2.00 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}) = 1.60 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{N}$. (b) The first electron moves in a straight line. The other two electrons take a circular path. (c) The first electron will never return to the origin. The other two will return. $$r = \frac{(9.11 \times 10^{-11})(5.00 \times 10^{7})}{(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(2.00 \times 10^{-7})}\ \text{m}, \qquad v = \frac{r}{t}, \qquad t = \frac{(9.11 \times 10^{-11})}{(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(2.00 \times 10^{-7})}\ \text{s} = 2.85 \times 10^{15}\ \text{s}$$
